blocks.text: About thirty kilometres east of the city of Mary, beside the town of Baýramaly, lie the ruins of Merv, *Merw* in Turkmen. UNESCO calls it the oldest and most completely preserved of the oasis cities along the Silk Roads in Central Asia, and it was added to the World Heritage List in 1999 as the State Historical and Cultural Park “Ancient Merv”, in Turkmen *Gadymy Merw*.

Merv grew up in the oasis of the Murgap river, where, according to UNESCO, people have lived in towns since the third millennium BCE. What a visitor sees today is not one city but several, built side by side over some two thousand years, each new city founded next to the last.

The oldest walled city, Erk Kala, goes back to the Persian Achaemenid empire, when Merv, called Margu in its inscriptions, was the seat of a province. Beside it rose Gyaur Kala, which the Seleucid king Antiochus I (who reigned 281–261 BCE) rebuilt as Antiochia Margiana; its remains include a Buddhist stupa and monastery. In the 7th century CE Arab armies took Merv and made it the capital of Khorasan, and under the Abbasid caliphs it became a great centre of Islamic learning. From that time date the Kyz Kalas, two fortified mud-brick houses with deeply ribbed walls.

Merv was at its height in the 11th and 12th centuries, as a capital of the Great Seljuk empire, in the new walled city of Sultan Kala. One historian of cities, Tertius Chandler, estimated that around 1150 it was the largest city in the world, with some 200,000 people. Its best-known building is from that time: the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, who ruled from 1118 to 1157, a square brick building 27 metres on each side under a great dome, once turquoise outside. In Turkmen it is *Soltan Sanjaryň kümmeti*.

In 1221 the Mongols took Merv and destroyed it. Medieval chroniclers wrote of hundreds of thousands of dead; their figures can't be checked, but the city never recovered. It was rebuilt in the 15th century without regaining its old prosperity, and the Russian Empire took the oasis in 1884.

blocks.title: Merw and Mary
blocks.text: The ancient city is *Merw*, the modern one *Mary*, and their endings differ: **to Merv** is *Merwe*, **to Mary** is *Mara* ([A1 unit 7](a1-u07)). **The Silk Road** is *Ýüpek ýoly*.
With this unit's future tense, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Geljek hepde biz Mara gitjek. Biz otly bilen gitjek. Gadymy Merw Marydan uzak däl. Men Soltan Sanjaryň kümmetini görjek. Biz Merwde iki gün galjak.
blocks.en: Next week we'll go to Mary. We'll go by train. Ancient Merv isn't far from Mary. I'll see the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar. We'll stay in Merv for two days.

questions.q: When was Ancient Merv added to the World Heritage List?
questions.explain: 1221 is when the Mongols destroyed the city, and 1157 is the end of Sultan Sanjar's reign.
*Soltan Sanjaryň* is the genitive: **Sultan Sanjar's**; *kümmeti* is **his mausoleum**.

questions.q: In the reading, how long will they stay in Merv?
questions.explain: *Biz Merwde iki gün galjak*: we'll stay in Merv for two days.

sources.title: State Historical and Cultural Park “Ancient Merv”
sources.note: The oldest and most completely preserved oasis city along the Silk Roads in Central Asia; urban centres in the Murgab oasis since the 3rd millennium BC; Erk Kala, Gyaur Kala with its Buddhist stupa and monastery, Sultan Kala walled in the 11th century, the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar (1118–57); capital of the Great Seljuk empire in the 11th–12th centuries

sources.title: Merv
sources.note: Near the modern town of Mary; Margu in cuneiform inscriptions, seat of an Achaemenid satrapy; capital of Khorasan from the 7th century; a centre of Islamic learning under the Abbasids; capital of Sanjar (reigned 1118–57); destroyed by the Mongols in 1221; rebuilt in the 15th century; occupied by the Russians in 1884

sources.title: Merv
sources.note: Inscribed in 1999; about 30 km east of Mary, by Baýramaly; Antiochus I (281–261 BC) and Antiochia Margiana; Tertius Chandler's estimate of 200,000 people by 1150; the Sanjar mausoleum, 27 m square, its exterior once turquoise; the Abbasid köşks (Greater and Lesser Gyzgala); chroniclers' death tolls for 1221
